A lithium ion battery includes a positive electrode and a negative electrode, and a nanoporous or microporous polymer separator soaked in an electrolyte solution and disposed between the electrodes. Comprising at least two different chelating agents and selected to complex with: i) two or more different transition metal ions; ii) transition metal ions in two or more different oxidation states; or iii) both i) and ii). The at least two different selected chelating agents complex with the transition metal ions in a manner sufficient to not affect movement of lithium ions through the separator during operation of the battery. Chelating agent: dissolved or dispersed in an electrolyte solution; a polymer grafted to the separator; a binder material attached to the negative electrode and/or the positive electrode; disposed within the aperture of the septum; coating on a surface of the separator; and/or coated on the surface of the electrode.

Lithium ion batteryTechnical Field

The present disclosure relates generally to lithium ion batteries.

Background

Secondary or rechargeable lithium ion batteries are used in many stationary and portable devices such as those encountered in the consumer electronics, automotive and aerospace industries. Lithium ion type batteries have gained popularity for a variety of reasons, including relatively high energy density, the general absence of any memory effect when compared to other types of rechargeable batteries, relatively low internal resistance, and low self-discharge rates when the battery is not in use. The ability of lithium batteries to undergo repeated charge-discharge cycles over their lifetime makes them an attractive and reliable source of electrical energy.

Disclosure of Invention

A lithium ion battery includes a positive electrode including a binder material, a negative electrode including a binder material, and a nanoporous or microporous polymer separator soaked in an electrolyte solution, the nanoporous or microporous polymer separator being operably disposed between the positive electrode and the negative electrode. At least two different chelating agents are included in the cell and are selected to complex with: i) two or more different transition metal ions; ii) transition metal ions in two or more different oxidation states; or iii) both i) and ii). The at least two different selected chelating agents complex with the transition metal ions in a manner sufficient to not affect movement of lithium ions through the nanoporous or microporous polymer membrane during operation of the lithium ion battery. The chelating agent is at least one of: dissolving in an electrolyte solution; grafted as a surrogate side group onto a polymer of a nanoporous or microporous polymer membrane; operably disposed within the aperture of the septum; a binder material attached to the negative electrode; a binder material attached to the positive electrode; coating on a surface of the separator; coating on the surface of the negative electrode; and coating on the surface of the positive electrode. The at least two different chelating agents are selected from the group of molecular form ion traps consisting of polyamines, thiols, and alkali metal salts of organic acids; polymers functionalized with alkali metal salts of organic acids; a polymer functionalized with a nitrogen-containing chemical group; a polymer functionalized with two or more functional groups; a polymer functionalized with a cyclic structure selected from the group consisting of: crown ethers, aza crown ethers, crypt ethers, lasso crown ethers, calixarenes, and combinations thereof.

Detailed Description

Lithium ion batteries generally operate by reversibly transferring lithium ions between a negative electrode (sometimes referred to as an anode) and a positive electrode (sometimes referred to as a cathode). The negative and positive electrodes are located on opposite sides of a porous polymer separator that is impregnated with an electrolyte solution suitable for conducting lithium ions. Each of the negative and positive electrodes is also operatively associated with or supported by its respective current collector. The current collectors associated with the two electrodes are connected, for example by tabs, to an interruptible external circuit that allows current to pass between the electrodes to electrically balance the associated migration of lithium ions. In addition, the anode may include a lithium intercalation host material, and the cathode may include a lithium-based active material that may store lithium ions at a higher potential than the intercalation host material of the anode. The electrolyte solution may contain a lithium salt dissolved in an aprotic nonaqueous solvent.

It has been found that lithium ion batteries are adversely affected by the elution of transition metal cations from the positive electrode, which results in accelerated capacity fade, resulting in a loss of durability in the battery. The transition metal cations migrate from the positive electrode to the negative electrode of the battery, causing it to be "poisoned". In one embodiment, the graphite electrode is from spinel Li of the positive electrodexMn2O4Active material dissolved Mn+2、Mn+3Or Mn+4Poisoning by cations. For example, Mn+2Cations may migrate through the battery electrolyte and deposit onto the graphite electrode. Mn when deposited on graphite+2The cation may become Mn metal. It has been shown that relatively small amounts (e.g., 90ppm) of Mn metal can poison graphite electrodes and prevent reversible electrode operation, thereby deleteriously affecting the service life of the battery. Whether exposure occurs through pure storage (i.e., stand alone at open circuit voltage at certain states of charge) or during battery operation (i.e., during charge, discharge, or charge-discharge cycles), the deleterious effects of Mn deposited on the negative electrode are significantly exacerbated when the battery is exposed to temperatures above ambient (e.g., above 40 ℃).

A chelating agent, separate from or bound to the polymer or ceramic material, complexes with and captures transition metal cations leached from the positive electrode of the lithium ion battery, thereby preventing their migration to the negative electrode and associated degradation of the battery performance. By using a selected/tailored mixture of transition metal ion chelating agents, e.g., a particular combination of Mn cations designed for use in at least two different oxidation states (and/or other combinations of transition metal cations) in a battery, a number of advantages exist. Some of these include: negative electrode poisoning by reduction/elimination of transition metal ions leached from the positive electrode; improved durability (cycle and calendar life) of lithium ion batteries; improving overall power performance by enabling battery operation at temperatures above ambient temperature; improved power performance below ambient temperature (-30 ℃); and by simplifying or potentially eliminating the lower system cost of the heat management system.

Inside the cell, the chelating agent effectively captures unwanted metal cations, while lithium ion movement across the nanoporous or microporous separator is unaffected during cell operation. In one embodiment, the chelating agent is formed, for example, by adding a metal cation (e.g., Co)+2、Fe+2、Mn+2Etc.) to selectively complex with unwanted metal cations that are dissolved in the electrolyte solution from the positive electrode. The chelating agent thus functions as a metal cation scavenger that traps and immobilizes unwanted metal cations to prevent the metal cations from migrating through the electrolyte solution and reaching the negative electrode. It will be appreciated that the chelating agent complexes less strongly with lithium ions (e.g. a single capture site out of every 100 sites is Li compared to the manganese cation+Cation occupancy) and therefore does not adversely affect the movement of lithium ions between the negative electrode and the positive electrode.

In fig. 1, the polymeric chelant forms the lithium ion battery separator 16. In this embodiment, the separator 16 itself is a porous film of polymeric chelant. In embodiments of the present disclosure, free (molecular) chelating agents 15 (i.e., not bound to the polymer) or polymeric chelating agents may also be used, for example, as a filler material within the membrane matrix and/or operably disposed within the pores 17 of the membrane 16 (e.g., as beads (separate from the membrane matrix) within the pores 17 of the membrane 16).

In another embodiment, the free (molecular) chelating agent 15 may also be dissolved or dispersed in the electrolyte solution.

In one embodiment, the chelating agent 15 attached to the polymer backbone 13 may be a crown ether, aza crown ether, crypt ether, crown ether having at least one ether oxygen substituted with a heteroatom, lasso crown ether, calixarene or a combination thereof. In addition, the size and shape of the lithium-ion battery 10, as well as the design and chemical composition of its major components, may vary depending on the particular application for which it is designed. For example, battery powered automobiles and handheld consumer electronics are two scenarios in which the lithium ion battery 10 is most likely designed to have different sizes, capacities, and power output specifications. The li-ion battery 10 or plurality of li-ion batteries may also be connected in series and/or parallel with other similar li-ion batteries to produce a greater voltage output and current (if arranged in parallel) or voltage (if arranged in series) if so desired by the load device 22.

Lithium-ion battery 10 generally operates by reversibly transferring lithium ions between a negative electrode 12 and a positive electrode 14. In the fully charged state, the voltage of the battery 10 is at a maximum (typically in the range of 2.0V-5.0V); while in the fully discharged state, the voltage of the battery 10 is at a minimum (typically in the range of 0V-2.0V). In essence, the fermi levels of the active materials in the positive and negative electrodes 14, 12 vary during operation of the battery, as does the difference between the two (also referred to as the battery voltage). The cell voltage decreases during discharge as the fermi levels approach each other. During charging, a process of reversal occurs, and as the fermi level is divided, the cell voltage increases. During battery discharge, the external load device 22 causes current to flow in one direction into the external circuit 18, thereby causing the difference between the fermi levels (and correspondingly, the battery voltage) to decrease. The opposite occurs during battery charging: the battery charger forces current to flow in one direction into the external circuit 18, thereby causing the difference between the fermi levels (and correspondingly, the battery voltage) to increase.

At the beginning of discharge, the negative electrode 12 of the lithium ion battery 10 contains a high concentration of intercalated lithium, while the positive electrode 14 is relatively depleted. When the negative electrode 12 contains a sufficiently higher relative content of intercalated lithium, the lithium ion battery 10 can generate a favorable current through a reversible electrochemical reaction that occurs when the external circuit 18 is closed to connect the negative electrode 12 and the positive electrode 14. In this case, the establishment of a closed external circuit causes the extraction of intercalated lithium from the negative electrode 12. When the extracted lithium atoms leave the intercalation host at the negative electrode-electrolyte interface, they are split into lithium ions (represented by black dots and open circles with a (+) charge) and electrons (e-).

The chemical potential difference between the positive electrode 14 and the negative electrode 12 (ranging from about 2.0V to 5.0V, depending on the precise chemical composition of the electrodes 14, 12) drives the electrons (e-) generated by oxidation of the intercalated lithium at the negative electrode 12 through an external circuit 18 to the positive electrode 14. Lithium ions also generated on the negative electrode 12 are simultaneously carried by the electrolyte solution through the porous separator 16 toward the positive electrode 14. The electrons (e-) flowing through the external circuit 18 and the lithium ions migrating through the separator 16 in the electrolyte solution eventually reconcile and form intercalated lithium on the positive electrode 14. The current through the external circuit 18 may be controlled and directed through the load device 22 until the level of intercalated lithium in the negative electrode 12 is below an operable level or the power demand is eliminated.

By applying an external battery charger to the lithium-ion battery 10 to reverse the electrochemical reactions that occur during battery discharge, the lithium-ion battery 10 can be charged or recharged at any time after its available capacity is partially or fully discharged. The connection of an external power source to the lithium ion battery 10 forces the lithium transition metal oxide or phosphate on the positive electrode 14 to otherwise undergo non-spontaneous oxidation, thereby generating electrons and releasing lithium ions. The electrons flowing back to the negative electrode 12 through the external circuit 18 and the lithium ions carried by the electrolyte through the microporous polymer membrane 16 toward the negative electrode 12 recombine on the negative electrode 12 and are replenished with intercalated lithium that is consumed during the next battery discharge cycle.

The external battery charger that may be used to charge the lithium-ion battery 10 may vary depending on the size, configuration, and particular end use of the lithium-ion battery 10. Some suitable external battery chargers include battery chargers that plug into ac outlets and automotive alternators.
